title: Your weekly rest
hook: design your digital sabbath: when, how long, what instead

segments.voice: Yesterday, companions, bread, and the phone nobody touched. Your line was eat with them. Which meal went screen-free? Day one hundred forty-seven.

Here's the week in one breath. Shabbat, the original weekly rest: a day off from making. Then one hour, phone in a drawer. Then the boredom that comes first, and the noticing after. Then one meal, eaten with the people instead of the feed. Now for the part that turns it from an experiment into a habit. You're going to design your own weekly rest. But first, one thing gets in almost everybody's way, and it's worth naming. It's the voice that says: you haven't done enough to deserve a break yet. Today's practice is your weekly rest.
screen: `SHABBAT, THE DRAWER, BOREDOM, THE MEAL.` → `NOT DONE ENOUGH YET?` → `YOUR WEEKLY REST.`

segments.voice: Notice something about the Sabbath we met at the start of this week. It doesn't wait for you to finish. It arrives at sunset on Friday whether the work is done or not. The medieval commentator Rashi, reading the command to work six days and do all your work, explains it this way: when the Sabbath comes, it should feel as if all your work is done. Not because it is. Because you're allowed to stop anyway. The Gospels have their own saying about it, in a different setting: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath." Each tradition keeps rest in its own way and for its own reasons. But both push against the same modern habit: treating rest as a prize for productivity. Rest isn't earned. It's part of the week. So, the design. Three questions. First, when? Pick a regular slot, like Saturday morning, or Sunday after lunch, or every weeknight after eight. Regular matters more than long. Second, how long? Start with what you'll actually keep. Three hours you keep beats a whole day you abandon. You can grow it. Third, and this is the one people forget: what instead? An empty rest fills right back up with scrolling. So choose what goes in the space: a walk, a long meal, a book, a nap, friends, prayer if you pray. Write down all three. A rest with a time, a length and a plan is much harder to skip than a vague good intention.
screen: `IT ARRIVES WHETHER YOU'RE DONE.` · `AS IF ALL YOUR WORK IS DONE.` · `WHEN, AND HOW LONG?` · `WHAT GOES IN INSTEAD?` · then, large: `REST ISN'T EARNED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: design your rest. Settle, and breathe. First, when: let a day and a time appear. Say it inside. Second, how long: pick a length you'd actually keep. Say it. Third, what instead: choose two things that will fill the space. Picture the rest beginning: phone into the drawer, a lamp on, a deep breath. Notice if the voice says you haven't earned it. Let it talk. Rest anyway. The bell holds the time.
Your weekly rest. A regular, screen-free stretch with a time, a length and a plan for what goes in it. Today's word.
Your line: rest isn't earned. Today, write your weekly rest down: when, how long, what instead. Put it somewhere you'll see it. Next week, we watch the sun go down. Day one hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: People who keep a digital sabbath usually set a regular weekly window, often an evening or a weekend day, put devices away, and plan what they'll do instead, like walks, meals, reading or rest.

original.note: Hebrew, menuchah: rest, repose. a word often used for the special rest of the Sabbath.

trapdoor: what you thought: rest is a reward for a productive week.
what it means: rest is part of the week, and it comes whether or not the work is done.
what a scholar hears: Rashi on Exodus 20:9 ('as if all your work were done'), drawing on the Mekhilta; and Mark 2:27.
